prompt: Write a note to a friend about a book you have been reading. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the note only.
final_message:
Hey Sam,

I finally picked up *The Overstory* by Richard Powers, the one you've been nagging me about since spring, and I owe you an apology for waiting. I'm about two-thirds through and I can't stop thinking about it.

I'll be honest: the first section nearly lost me. It's a run of short, separate stories about nine people, and each one gets a tree. A Brooklyn family photographs the same chestnut every generation. A soldier is saved by a banyan. A woman builds a quiet, strange life around a botanist's obsession. I kept wondering when they'd all connect. Then they started to meet, and the book changed. It went from a collection of portraits to something with real momentum and stakes.

What's stayed with me most is how Powers writes about trees. They stop being scenery. There's a passage about how forests share nutrients and warnings through their roots and fungi. He doesn't treat it as a neat fact. He treats it as a way to think about time. We live in decades, and a tree lives in centuries. Walking past the big oak on my street felt different afterward. I stood there like an idiot, looking up.

The activism thread is the part I'm still arguing with. The characters who chain themselves to old growth are written with so much love that I wanted them to win, and the book is clear-eyed about what that fight costs them. It doesn't flinch, and it doesn't preach, even though it could have. I've read plenty of novels with a message where the message flattens the people. Here the people stay complicated, stubborn and sometimes wrong, and I trust the book more for it.

One warning, since I know your taste. The prose is dense in places, and a few of the scientific stretches slow things down. I skimmed one of them and didn't feel bad. If you want a fast plot, this isn't it. If you want something that gets into your head and rearranges the furniture, it is.

I won't spoil the ending, partly because I haven't reached it. If anyone dies I'm blaming you.

Can we get coffee soon so I can hear whether you cried at the same place I did? Bring your copy if you still have it. I want to see what you underlined.

Talk soon,
[name]
